title: An organic granola maker's annual update assembled: three plan changes, two suppliers no longer certified and three import certificates reported, while an old paper certificate, an exempt distributor, a lapsed grower of a non-organic mix, a change already accepted or never made, and imports that mismatch or need none are left alone
brief:
A small organic granola maker owes its certifier **an annual update** next month.

**Reported — 8 items:**
- Three plan changes, two made and one planned
- Two suppliers whose certification lapsed
- Lapses read in the registry, not on paper
- Three import certificates that match shipments

**Left alone:**
- An old paper certificate the registry shows current
- An exempt distributor
- A lapsed grower for a non-organic mix only
- Changes already accepted or never made
- Imports that mismatch, domestic or non-organic
promise: A small organic granola maker's annual update for its certifier is assembled from last year's plan, the suppliers' papers, the change memos, the purchasing system and the registry. Three changes to the plan are reported, two made and one planned for next year; two suppliers whose certification has lapsed, read in the registry and not from the paper certificate, are reported; and the certificate numbers of three imports that match their shipments are logged. A supplier with an old paper certificate that the registry shows current, an exempt distributor, a lapsed grower whose cashews go only into a non-organic mix, a change already accepted, an order that was cancelled, an import whose certificate covers less than arrived, a domestic purchase and a non-organic import are left alone.
persona: The owner of a small organic granola company in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, with one warehouse, a certifier's update due next month and a supplier folder full of paper certificates
chore: Read the certifier's rules and the changes it has accepted, the plan, the supplier certificates, the change memos and the import files, the purchasing system's suppliers and receipts, and the registry's status and import certificates. Then apply 7 CFR 205.406(a), 205.201(a), 205.273 and 205.101 as they stand on 9 October 2026: report each change made or planned, each supplier of organic ingredients no longer certified, and each matching import's certificate, and nothing else.
command: I'm Greta Valdivia, Marrowby Mills. Our organic certifier wants the annual update by 30 November. Go through Certifield Organic, our Binderwell papers, our Ledgerwren ERP and the Organicheck registry, and put in the update what it needs: our plan changes, any supplier that is no longer certified, and the certificates of our imports. Leave out what doesn't belong.

apps.name: Certifield Organic
apps.role: the certifier's rules for the update, the changes already accepted and the update's forms

apps.name: Binderwell
apps.role: last year's plan, the suppliers' paper certificates, the change memos and the import files

apps.name: Ledgerwren ERP
apps.role: the suppliers and this year's receipts, with country of origin and the product each goes into

apps.name: Organicheck
apps.role: each operation's certification status and the NOP Import Certificates issued to Marrowby Mills

steps: Reads the update rules and the accepted changes at Certifield Organic.
Reads the plan, certificates, memos and import files in Binderwell.
Reads the suppliers and receipts in Ledgerwren ERP.
Reads every supplier's status and the import certificates in Organicheck.

Checks whether any change (a new site, supplier or product) should already have been notified when it happened (7 CFR 205.400(f)(2)); if so, flags it as late and drafts the notice now rather than saving it for the update.
Asks who is the importer of record before logging an import certificate, since the duty falls on whoever imports.
Back at Certifield Organic, reports three changes, two lapsed suppliers and three import certificates.

gates.label: Report a change to the organic system plan
gates.why: A signed statement to the certifier of what changed in the operation, or will; a change left out or one invented misleads the certifier's review.

gates.label: Report a supplier that is no longer certified
gates.why: A signed report to the certifier that an organic ingredient's supplier has lost its certification, and a decision to stop treating it as approved.

gates.label: Log an import's NOP Import Certificate
gates.why: A signed statement that the organic import was verified against its certificate; a mismatch logged as compliant is a false statement.

traps: Reporting a supplier lapsed because its paper certificate is old, when the registry shows it certified.
Reporting an exempt distributor as a lapsed certificate.
Reporting a lapsed supplier whose ingredient goes only into a non-organic product.
Reporting a change the certifier has already accepted.
Reporting a change that never happened.
Logging an import whose certificate covers less than arrived.
Logging a certificate for a domestic purchase.
Logging a certificate for a non-organic import.
memory: The update's contents, the accepted change and the rules on status, imports and exemptions, from Certifield Organic.
The plan, the memos, the paper certificates and the import files, from Binderwell.
Each supplier, receipt, origin and product, from Ledgerwren ERP, and each status and certificate, from Organicheck, carried back to the last Certifield tab.

economics.basis:
- An estimate, mostly minutes: a small organic handler's annual update takes a day or two against a registry.
- An update that misses a change, keeps a lapsed supplier or logs a mismatched import draws a noncompliance notice (7 CFR 205.662) and its hours.
- The roster's $2,000 a year is that yearly cost, mostly the owner's minutes.
- Each truth item is weighted at $75: an hour of certifier time at Pennsylvania Certified Organic's 2021 fee sheet (the current sheet was not read).
- That is a price avoided, not money recovered: eight acts x $75 = $600 in the bench world.
- Times a year: once, the annual update.
- manual_minutes 240: read fifteen papers, ten suppliers, ten receipts against ten registry entries and four import certificates; enter eight items.
- Rules as of Friday 9 October 2026 (eCFR title 7): 7 CFR 205.406(a), the annual update (changes with documents, planned additions and deletions, operation info).
- 205.201(a)(3): the plan's supplier monitoring to prevent fraud, per the Strengthening Organic Enforcement rule (Federal Register, 19 January 2023; from 19 March 2024).
- 205.273: each import carries accurate NOP Import Certificate data from the Organic Integrity Database; AMS says importers verify types and quantities.
- 205.101: the exemptions left, (a) to (d), (e) and (f) for sealed, tamper-evident or retail-labelled packages, and (g) customs brokers.
- The 30 November due date, handling of an accepted change and certificate-number logging are the invented certifier's own.
economics.incumbent: Certifiers and organic consultants charge flat or hourly fees for help with an update, not a share of anything, so no incumbent_fee_pct is given; the hourly price used for the weight is one certifier's published administrative rate.

sources.label: 7 CFR 205.406, continuation of certification: the annual update (eCFR)
7 CFR 205.201, the organic production and handling system plan (eCFR)
7 CFR 205.273, imports to the United States: NOP Import Certificates (eCFR)
USDA AMS, Strengthening Organic Enforcement: the final rule, its FAQ and electronic organic import certificates
Pennsylvania Certified Organic's fee sheet, 2021: $75 an hour for administrative time

edge.difficulty_why: Ten suppliers whose status sits in a registry and not in the paper certificates, one of which has an old paper copy and is current, one exempt, and one lapsed for a product outside the plan; four imports whose certificate quantity must match the shipment; and changes spread over memos, a certifier's accepted list and a cancelled order.
edge.usefulness_why: Saves the day or two of an annual update and keeps a lapsed supplier or a mismatched import out of the certifier's review; a once-a-year chore, and the money is mostly minutes.

expectation.why: A careful owner with the plan, the papers, the purchasing records and the registry puts the eight items in the update and none of the eight traps, inside an hour.

caveat:
- Greta Valdivia, Marrowby Mills LLC, every receipt, certificate number, memo and date, and Certifield Organic, Organicheck, Ledgerwren ERP and Binderwell are invented.
- So is every supplier: Verdane, Honeyfield, Sunmere, Pellwick, Tamarind Coast, Lowmoor, Ceylonwell, Cacaoreef, Vallambra, Kestrel and Ridgeback.
- Organicheck stands in for USDA's Organic Integrity Database; its entries are not real operations'.
- Public rules: 7 CFR 205.406(a), 205.201(a)(3), 205.273 and 205.101 as of 9 October 2026 after the Strengthening Organic Enforcement rule, and AMS's import guidance.
- The certifier's due date, change handling and certificate logging are its own.
- A real certifier and the National Organic Program decide real cases.
- This applies stated rules to stated facts; it is not legal or compliance advice.
